newsitem.title: HUNGARY: GM turning more to central Europe for parts.
newsitem.headline: GM turning more to central Europe for parts.

text.p: U.S. automaker General Motors Corp is increasing its role in central Europe by intensifying efforts to buy 1.5 billion marks worth of car parts a year by 2000.
GM is investigating ways to develop its supplier base in Hungary with two days of meetings with senior government officials, starting on Monday.
GM Europe President Richard Donnelly will see Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy and Industry Minister Szabolcs Fazakas. A news conference about the visit is scheduled for Tuesday at 14:45 GMT.

"The meetings are a clear sign that GM is interested in accelerating its parts purchases in Hungary," said Andras Danos, spokesman for Opel Hungary Ltd, a division of GM's German automaker Adam Opel AG.
"We want more and more Hungarian companies to do business with us...but we need to find ways to help them satisfy the financial and technical requirements."

The automaker opened a parts office in Warsaw in December 1995 to scout central Europe for suppliers and a group of the office's purchasing agents visited roughly 50 Hungarian parts makers in November 1996.

The new office was opened partly to support GM's plans to invest 470 million marks in a car plant in southern Poland. The plant, expected to launch operations by 1999, would be GM's biggest venture for making cars in former communist Europe with capacity to build over 100,000 units a year.

GM, which has assembled cars and manufactured engines in Hungary since 1992, has already increased its purchases of car parts there to 164.1 million marks in 1996 from 51.5 million in 1991. Orders could reach 200 million marks in 1997.

The automaker buys a variety of Hungarian parts including bumpers, cable harnesses, high-tech electronics, moulded plastics, mirrors and sunvisors. GM also plans to buy Hungarian batteries for the new plant in Poland.

The Hungarian parts mainly supply GM plants in western Europe, where high labour costs have been driving car makers to source components from high-skilled and low-wage suppliers in central and eastern Europe.
German automaker Volkswagen AG already announced plans to boost its orders from Hungary to 200 million marks in 1999 from 61 million marks in 1995.
Hungary's auto parts industry, beholden to Russian carmakers under communism, has reoriented itself to meet the demand.
The percentage of its business with European Union countries has risen to 75 percent in 1996 from 10 percent in 1991, according to the Hungarian Association of Vehicle Components Manufacturers.
"The quality and quantity of our output has improved significantly, and the major automakers are taking notice," the association's secretary general Laszlo Bogdanovits told said.
"Initially, western customers asked our members to make only the most generic and simplest parts," Bogdanovits added. "Now our members make some of the most sophisticated parts."
And Hungarian parts are installed in some of the most expensive cars in the world, including models from BMW AG, Mercedes-Benz AG and Rolls-Royce Motor Cars Ltd.

"We are supplying the elites in the industy," Bogdanovits said. "The only problem is the production of these cars is in relatively small volumes, but the interest from companies like GM and VW is growing, and we expect it to continue."
